questions.questionText: Your organization runs a nightly batch processing workload on Compute Engine that takes 4 hours to complete. The workload is highly fault-tolerant and can automatically resume if interrupted. Which Compute Engine pricing model should you choose to minimize costs?

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs are available at up to a 91% discount compared to standard instances. They are ideal for fault-tolerant and batch workloads because Google Cloud can reclaim the instances at any time if it needs the capacity.

why other options are wrong.On-demand instances: On-demand instances are the most expensive option and are meant for unpredictable, non-interruptible workloads.
why other options are wrong.Committed Use Discounts (1-year): CUDs require a 1-year or 3-year commitment for 24/7 workloads. A 4-hour nightly job would leave the reserved capacity wasted for 20 hours a day.
why other options are wrong.Sustained Use Discounts: SUDs apply automatically when a VM runs for a significant portion of the billing month. A 4-hour daily run does not qualify for meaningful SUDs.

questions.questionText: Your company stores millions of user-uploaded images in Cloud Storage Standard class. Analytics show that images older than 90 days are rarely accessed (less than once a year). You want to optimize storage costs without requiring any application code changes. What should you do?
options: Configure an Object Lifecycle Management rule to move objects older than 90 days to the Archive storage class.
Write a Cloud Function triggered by a Cloud Scheduler to copy older objects to a new bucket.
Change the default storage class of the bucket to Coldline.
Enable Object Versioning on the bucket.
correctAnswers: Configure an Object Lifecycle Management rule to move objects older than 90 days to the Archive storage class.

explanation.general explanation: Object Lifecycle Management allows you to define rules that automatically transition objects to cheaper storage classes (like Coldline or Archive) based on conditions such as object age. This is native, fully managed, and requires no code changes.

why other options are wrong.Write a Cloud Function triggered by a Cl: This introduces operational overhead, custom code, and API costs, which are completely unnecessary since Lifecycle policies do this natively.
why other options are wrong.Change the default storage class of the: Changing the default class only affects newly uploaded objects; it does not change the class of existing objects.
Versioning retains deleted or overwritten objects, which actually increases storage costs.

questions.questionText: You are migrating a steady-state monolithic application to Google Cloud. The application must run 24/7 continuously, and the compute resource requirements are highly predictable. You want to achieve the lowest possible Compute Engine compute cost for this workload. Which pricing plan should you adopt?
options: On-demand pricing with Sustained Use Discounts (SUDs)

explanation.general explanation: For predictable, continuous (24/7) steady-state workloads, a 3-year Committed Use Discount provides the highest percentage of cost savings (up to 57% or more) compared to 1-year CUDs or standard on-demand pricing.

why other options are wrong.Spot VMs: Spot VMs are cheaper but are preemptible. A steady-state monolithic application generally cannot tolerate random interruptions without downtime.
why other options are wrong.1-year Committed Use Discounts (CUDs): While 1-year CUDs save money, the 3-year commitment offers a significantly deeper discount.
why other options are wrong.On-demand pricing with Sustained Use Dis: SUDs apply automatically up to 30%, but 3-year CUDs offer much larger discounts and are the best choice for a workload with known 24/7 requirements.

questions.questionText: Your data science team runs queries in BigQuery using the on-demand pricing model. They frequently query a large table containing 5 years of log data, but usually only filter for the last 7 days. Their queries are currently scanning the entire table, resulting in high costs. What is the most effective way to reduce the query costs?
options: Export the table to Cloud Storage and query it using external tables.
Partition the BigQuery table by the timestamp column.
Change the BigQuery pricing model to capacity-based pricing.
Create a secondary index on the timestamp column.
correctAnswers: Partition the BigQuery table by the timestamp column.

explanation.general explanation: Partitioning a table by a date/timestamp column divides a large table into smaller segments. When queries include a filter on the partitioned column, BigQuery only scans the partitions that match the filter, drastically reducing the bytes read and the associated cost in the on-demand pricing model.

why other options are wrong.Export the table to Cloud Storage and qu: Querying external tables is generally slower and often more expensive because external queries still scan the data, and you lose BigQuery's native optimizations.
why other options are wrong.Change the BigQuery pricing model to cap: Switching to capacity pricing provides predictable costs, but it doesn't optimize the actual query inefficiency. Partitioning should be done first to reduce resource consumption.
why other options are wrong.Create a secondary index on the timestam: BigQuery is a columnar database and does not use traditional secondary indexes like a relational database. It relies on partitioning and clustering.

questions.questionText: Your application has users globally, but latency is not a critical factor. You want to reduce the outbound internet egress costs of routing traffic from your Google Cloud resources to your end users. Which Google Cloud networking feature should you configure?

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud offers two Network Service Tiers. The Standard tier routes outbound traffic over the public internet as quickly as possible, bypassing Google's private network backbone. It provides lower network egress costs at the expense of potentially higher latency and lower performance, making it ideal for non-critical, cost-sensitive workloads.

why other options are wrong.Premium Network Service Tier: Premium Tier routes traffic over Google's high-performance global backbone. It is more reliable and faster but comes at a higher cost.
why other options are wrong.Cloud VPN: Cloud VPN connects on-premises networks to GCP; it is not used to route general internet traffic to end users.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Interconnect: Cloud Interconnect provides a dedicated physical connection to on-premises environments, not to general internet end users.

questions.questionText: You are auditing a Google Cloud project to identify cost-saving opportunities. You suspect that many Compute Engine virtual machines are over-provisioned (e.g., they have 8 vCPUs but only utilize 10% on average). Which built-in GCP feature will automatically identify these instances and suggest cheaper alternatives?

explanation.general explanation: Compute Engine provides Rightsizing Recommendations automatically via the Recommender service. It analyzes CPU and memory utilization over the last 8 days and suggests resizing instances to smaller machine types if they are consistently underutilized, directly reducing costs.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Profiler: Cloud Profiler analyzes application code performance (CPU/memory usage of specific functions), not whole VM infrastructure rightsizing.
why other options are wrong.Google Cloud Pricing Calculator: The Pricing Calculator is a manual estimation tool used before deployment; it does not analyze running resources.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Monitoring Uptime Checks: Uptime checks verify if a service is accessible via the internet, completely unrelated to resource sizing.

questions.questionText: You have a microservice that processes webhooks. Traffic is extremely sporadic, sometimes going to zero for hours, and then spiking briefly. You want to host this containerized service with the absolute lowest cost when there is no traffic. Which service should you choose?

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Run is a fully managed serverless platform for containerized applications. It automatically scales to zero instances when there are no incoming requests. Since you only pay for the exact CPU/memory consumed during request processing (down to 100 millisecond increments), scaling to zero results in zero compute costs during idle periods.

why other options are wrong.Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Autopilot: While Autopilot scales dynamically, there is always a minimum cost overhead for the cluster control plane and running pods.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine Managed Instance Group: MIGs can autoscale, but scaling to zero is typically more complex to manage with traditional VMs, and you pay for minimum running instances by default.
why other options are wrong.App Engine Flexible: App Engine Flexible requires at least one instance running continuously and does not scale to zero.

questions.questionText: An application requires 6 vCPUs and exactly 10 GB of RAM. The standard pre-defined machine types available are either n2-standard-4 (4 vCPU, 16 GB) or n2-standard-8 (8 vCPU, 32 GB). How can you provision a VM that exactly meets the requirements to avoid paying for unneeded resources?
options: Provision an n2-standard-8 and under-clock the CPUs using a startup script.
Use a Custom Machine Type to specify exactly 6 vCPUs and 10 GB of RAM.
Provision two n2-standard-4 instances and cluster them.
Deploy the application on Cloud Run and set memory limits.
correctAnswers: Use a Custom Machine Type to specify exactly 6 vCPUs and 10 GB of RAM.

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud allows you to create Custom Machine Types. If standard machine types don't fit your workload, you can define the exact number of vCPUs and the exact amount of memory you need. This prevents over-provisioning and saves money.

why other options are wrong.Provision an n2-standard-8 and under-clo: You still pay Google for the n2-standard-8 configuration regardless of how you configure the OS internally.
why other options are wrong.Provision two n2-standard-4 instances an: This provides 8 vCPUs and 32 GB RAM total, which over-provisions resources and increases architectural complexity.
why other options are wrong.Deploy the application on Cloud Run and: While possible depending on the app, the prompt specifically discusses optimizing VM sizing based on exact hardware requirements.

questions.questionText: The finance department wants to ensure they are immediately notified if the monthly spend on a specific Google Cloud project exceeds $1,000. What native Google Cloud billing feature should you configure?
options: A daily Cloud Scheduler job to query the Billing API

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Billing Budgets and Alerts allow you to set financial limits for projects or billing accounts. You can configure alert thresholds (e.g., 50%, 90%, 100% of the $1,000 budget) to automatically send email notifications or trigger Pub/Sub messages when the spend exceeds those thresholds.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Monitoring Uptime Checks: Uptime checks are for tracking application availability, not financial spend.
why other options are wrong.Billing Data Export to BigQuery: Exporting to BigQuery is used for deep analysis and building dashboards, but it does not natively send real-time budget threshold alerts.
why other options are wrong.A daily Cloud Scheduler job to query the: Building a custom application to poll the API is unnecessary when Budgets and Alerts provide this functionality natively and securely out of the box.

questions.questionText: You are hosting a web application on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). During the day, the application needs 20 nodes to handle traffic. At night, it only needs 3 nodes. You want to optimize costs by automatically removing idle compute nodes at night. Which GKE feature should you enable?

explanation.general explanation: The GKE Cluster Autoscaler automatically resizes the number of nodes in a node pool based on the demands of your workloads. If nodes are underutilized and their pods can be scheduled onto other nodes in the cluster, it will delete the idle nodes to save costs.

why other options are wrong.Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA): VPA adjusts the CPU and memory requests/limits of individual pods, not the underlying compute nodes.
why other options are wrong.Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA): HPA scales the number of pods up or down based on metrics like CPU utilization. While HPA decreases pods at night, it is the Cluster Autoscaler that actually deletes the empty nodes to save money.
why other options are wrong.Node Auto-Provisioning (NAP): NAP automatically creates new node pools with sizing optimized for pending pods. Standard Cluster Autoscaler is the mechanism for removing idle nodes from existing pools.

questions.questionText: Your company wants to perform a deep analysis of its Google Cloud spending to understand exactly which microservices and labels are accumulating the highest costs over the past year. What is the Google-recommended approach to enable this analysis?
options: Download the monthly PDF invoices from the Cloud Console.
Enable Cloud Billing export to BigQuery.
Use Cloud Logging to filter by 'billing' events.
Set up a Cloud Function to scrape the Billing API daily and store it in Cloud SQL.
correctAnswers: Enable Cloud Billing export to BigQuery.

explanation.general explanation: Enabling Cloud Billing export to BigQuery automatically sends granular, daily billing data (including labels and specific resource usage) to a BigQuery dataset. From there, you can write complex SQL queries or connect to Looker Studio for deep cost analysis.

why other options are wrong.Download the monthly PDF invoices from t: PDF invoices provide an aggregate summary and cannot be dynamically analyzed or broken down by specific resource labels.
why other options are wrong.Use Cloud Logging to filter by 'billing': Cloud Logging records operational and audit events. It does not store financial billing metrics.
why other options are wrong.Set up a Cloud Function to scrape the Bi: This is an unnecessary custom engineering effort. BigQuery export is the native, fully managed, and standard best practice for billing analysis.

questions.questionText: To prevent accidental run-away costs in BigQuery, your engineering manager wants to ensure that a single query cannot accidentally process an entire 10 TB table when someone forgets a WHERE clause. What setting should you enforce on the project's BigQuery queries?
options: Set a strict Identity and Access Management (IAM) quota on the user account.
Create a Cloud Run service to pre-validate all queries before execution.

explanation.general explanation: BigQuery allows you to set a 'Maximum bytes billed' limit either at the project level, user level, or query level. If a query is estimated to scan more bytes than the specified limit, BigQuery will immediately fail the query without running it, preventing unexpected charges.

why other options are wrong.Enable BigQuery Reservations capacity pr: Capacity pricing charges a flat monthly rate, which solves the financial risk of a single query, but it changes the entire billing model of the organization which may not be desired or cost-effective.
why other options are wrong.Set a strict Identity and Access Managem: IAM controls permissions (who can query), not the data volume a query scans.
why other options are wrong.Create a Cloud Run service to pre-valida: This is a complex, custom, and unnecessary solution. BigQuery provides the dry-run and bytes billed limits natively.

questions.questionText: You are migrating a small, internal wiki application to Compute Engine. The application serves very little traffic, but must remain online. You want to choose the most cost-effective machine type family that allows the CPU to temporarily burst above its baseline when occasionally needed. Which machine family should you choose?

explanation.general explanation: E2 Shared-Core machine types (e.g., e2-micro, e2-small) provide a fraction of a vCPU continuously and are capable of bursting to full vCPUs for short periods. They are highly cost-effective and designed specifically for small, low-traffic workloads like microservices or internal applications.

why other options are wrong.C2 Compute-Optimized: C2 instances provide dedicated, high-frequency CPUs for intensive workloads like gaming or HPC. They are expensive and inappropriate for a small internal wiki.
why other options are wrong.M2 Memory-Optimized: M2 instances are for massive in-memory databases (like SAP HANA) and are among the most expensive VM types.
why other options are wrong.A2 Accelerator-Optimized: A2 instances are for machine learning workloads requiring attached GPUs. They are very expensive.

questions.questionText: Your team relies heavily on Compute Engine instances for rendering video frames. The rendering software is robust; if a VM is suddenly shut down, another VM simply picks up the abandoned frame. What compute option should you use to drastically reduce the cost of this rendering farm?

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs are spare compute capacity offered by Google at heavily discounted prices (up to 91%). Google can preempt (terminate) them at any time. Because the rendering software is fault-tolerant and can recover from interruptions without data loss, Spot VMs are the perfect, highly cost-optimized solution.

why other options are wrong.Dedicated Hosts / Sole-tenant nodes: These options reserve dedicated physical hardware for compliance or licensing reasons. They are more expensive than standard multi-tenant VMs.
why other options are wrong.Shielded VMs: Shielded VMs provide enhanced security (verifiable boot, vTPM) against rootkits. They do not intrinsically provide cost discounts for interruptible workloads.

questions.questionText: You are hosting a static website on Cloud Storage. The site has unexpectedly gone viral, resulting in terabytes of outbound network traffic per day. To reduce the massive Cloud Storage network egress charges, what should you place in front of the Cloud Storage bucket?

explanation.general explanation: Cloud CDN caches content at the Google network edge, close to the users. When content is served from the CDN cache, you pay lower CDN egress rates instead of the higher origin egress rates from Cloud Storage. This drastically reduces overall network egress costs for static, heavily accessed content.

why other options are wrong.Cloud NAT: Cloud NAT allows internal, private VMs to access the public internet. It does not cache inbound user requests.
why other options are wrong.Cloud VPN: Cloud VPN connects on-premises networks to GCP; it does not optimize public internet traffic delivery.
why other options are wrong.Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP): IAP controls secure access to web applications based on user identity. It does not perform content caching or reduce network egress costs.

questions.questionText: Your application generates monthly reporting PDFs that must be stored for exactly one year for compliance. The reports are accessed frequently during the first month, but almost never accessed afterward. How should you optimize Cloud Storage costs?
options: Upload the PDFs initially to the Standard storage class.
Upload the PDFs initially to the Archive storage class.
Use an Object Lifecycle rule to transition objects to Nearline or Coldline after 30 days.
Use an Object Lifecycle rule to transition objects to Standard after 30 days.
correctAnswers: Upload the PDFs initially to the Standard storage class.
Use an Object Lifecycle rule to transition objects to Nearline or Coldline after 30 days.

explanation.general explanation: Because the objects are accessed frequently in the first month, they should be placed in the Standard storage class to avoid early retrieval fees and high operations costs associated with colder tiers. After 30 days, when access becomes rare, an Object Lifecycle rule should automatically transition them to a colder, cheaper tier (like Nearline or Coldline) to optimize long-term storage costs.

why other options are wrong.Upload the PDFs initially to the Archive: Archive class has high retrieval fees and minimum storage durations. Accessing them frequently in the first month would result in massive cost penalties.
why other options are wrong.Use an Object Lifecycle rule to transiti: Transitioning to Standard after 30 days would move the data to the most expensive tier precisely when it is no longer being accessed, increasing costs.

questions.questionText: Your development team uses dozens of high-performance Compute Engine VMs for testing. These environments are only used Monday through Friday from 9 AM to 5 PM. What is the simplest and most automated way to stop paying for these compute instances during nights and weekends?
options: Use an Instance Group and manually resize it to zero every evening.
Implement Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Cloud Function that stops and starts the instances on a schedule.
Convert the development VMs to Spot VMs.
Delete the VMs every evening and recreate them from scratch using Terraform.
correctAnswers: Implement Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Cloud Function that stops and starts the instances on a schedule.

explanation.general explanation: Stopping a Compute Engine instance halts the CPU and memory billing. A standard, simple pattern in GCP is using Cloud Scheduler to send a Pub/Sub message or HTTP request to a Cloud Function, which then automatically stops instances tagged with 'development' at 5 PM and starts them at 9 AM.

why other options are wrong.Use an Instance Group and manually resiz: Manual processes are prone to human error. The goal is an automated solution.
Spot VMs can be preempted at any time, which would constantly interrupt the developers' work during the day.
why other options are wrong.Delete the VMs every evening and recreat: While valid for highly mature CI/CD setups (ephemeral environments), stopping/starting is vastly simpler to implement for existing stateful dev machines.

questions.questionText: Your enterprise organization's BigQuery usage has grown rapidly. Multiple departments run hundreds of complex queries daily. The CFO is complaining about highly variable and unpredictable monthly bills under the on-demand pricing model. What should you recommend?
options: Disable BigQuery and migrate data to Cloud SQL.
Implement BigQuery capacity-based (flat-rate) pricing using Reservations.
Set the maximum bytes billed to 1 GB for all queries.
Export all BigQuery data to Cloud Storage Standard class.
correctAnswers: Implement BigQuery capacity-based (flat-rate) pricing using Reservations.

explanation.general explanation: BigQuery capacity-based pricing (formerly flat-rate via Reservations) allows organizations to purchase dedicated query processing capacity (slots). You pay a flat, predictable fee for these slots regardless of how many bytes are scanned, effectively eliminating variable monthly bills.

why other options are wrong.Disable BigQuery and migrate data to Clo: Cloud SQL is a relational OLTP database, not a replacement for BigQuery's petabyte-scale data warehouse analytics capabilities.
why other options are wrong.Set the maximum bytes billed to 1 GB for: This would cause almost all complex enterprise queries to fail, disrupting the business.
why other options are wrong.Export all BigQuery data to Cloud Storag: You cannot run complex SQL analytics natively and quickly on Cloud Storage without external tables or a query engine like BigQuery.

questions.questionText: You are designing a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) architecture for a set of background worker microservices. These services pull messages from Pub/Sub, process them, and are highly fault-tolerant. You want to run this node pool at the lowest possible cost. What node pool configuration is best?
options: Create a node pool using dedicated host machines.
Create a node pool configured to use Spot VMs.
Create a node pool using Compute-Optimized (C2) instances.
correctAnswers: Create a node pool configured to use Spot VMs.

explanation.general explanation: GKE allows you to provision node pools specifically composed of Spot VMs. Since the background worker microservices are fault-tolerant and pull from a message queue (Pub/Sub), they can gracefully handle the underlying Spot VMs being preempted. This offers massive cost savings (up to 91%).

why other options are wrong.Create a node pool using dedicated host: Dedicated hosts are for compliance and license isolation; they increase costs.
why other options are wrong.Create a node pool using Compute-Optimiz: C2 instances are premium, expensive VMs designed for high-performance computing, not background cost-optimized processing.
Shielded nodes provide enhanced boot security, not cost reduction.

questions.questionText: Your company currently has a hybrid cloud architecture. You transfer huge amounts of data (several Petabytes monthly) from Google Cloud to your on-premises data center over a standard Cloud VPN connected via the public internet. Egress costs are heavily impacting the budget. How can you significantly reduce the per-GB network egress costs?
options: Enable Cloud NAT for the VPC.
Switch from Cloud VPN to Dedicated Interconnect.
Upgrade the Cloud VPN to High Availability (HA) VPN.
Compress the data using Cloud CDN.
correctAnswers: Switch from Cloud VPN to Dedicated Interconnect.

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud offers significantly discounted egress pricing for traffic routed over Cloud Interconnect (Dedicated or Partner) compared to standard internet egress (which is what Cloud VPN uses). For multi-petabyte transfers, the cost of the physical Dedicated Interconnect circuit is vastly outweighed by the per-GB egress savings.

Cloud NAT allows internal IPs to access the internet; it does not change the per-GB billing rate of internet egress.
why other options are wrong.Upgrade the Cloud VPN to High Availabili: HA VPN improves reliability (SLA) but still uses the public internet and standard internet egress pricing.
Cloud CDN caches HTTP(s) objects at the edge for external users; it is not used for backend data center replication.

questions.questionText: A team queries a large, heavily partitioned BigQuery table. However, they frequently apply a WHERE clause to filter by the 'customer_id' column inside specific partitions. The queries are still scanning more data than necessary within the partition. What feature can you use to organize data within partitions to reduce data scanned and lower costs?

explanation.general explanation: Clustering sorts the data within a BigQuery table (or within its partitions) based on the contents of one or more specified columns (e.g., 'customer_id'). When a query filters by a clustered column, BigQuery uses block signatures to skip scanning blocks that don't match, drastically reducing bytes scanned and costs.

why other options are wrong.Materialized Views: Materialized views precompute results. While useful for aggregations, clustering is the direct method for sorting raw table data to optimize filter lookups.
why other options are wrong.Dataflow Streaming: Dataflow is a processing engine for ETL, not a BigQuery query optimization feature.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Bigtable secondary indexes: Bigtable is a NoSQL database and entirely separate from BigQuery analytics.

questions.questionText: You are deploying a Node.js web application to App Engine Standard environment. You want to ensure that sudden spikes in malicious traffic or DDOS attempts do not cause the autoscaler to spin up hundreds of instances, resulting in a massive unapproved bill. What configuration setting should you apply?
options: Configure Cloud Armor to block all international IP addresses.
Deploy the application on App Engine Flexible instead.

explanation.general explanation: In the App Engine Standard environment, you can define a `max_instances` setting in the `app.yaml` configuration file. This places a hard ceiling on how many instances the platform will autoscale to, serving as a primary cost-control mechanism against sudden traffic spikes.

why other options are wrong.Configure Cloud Armor to block all inter: Cloud Armor protects against DDOS, but blocking all international IPs degrades legitimate global access and is not a direct autoscaling limit.
Manual scaling requires you to provision instances constantly, losing the cost benefits of scaling to zero during low traffic periods.
why other options are wrong.Deploy the application on App Engine Fle: App Engine Flexible is generally more expensive than Standard, does not scale to zero, and does not inherently prevent runaway scaling.

questions.questionText: Your GKE cluster uses the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA), but you notice that many pods are deployed with requested CPU values of 2 vCPUs when they actually only use 0.1 vCPUs. This causes the cluster autoscaler to aggressively add expensive nodes. Which feature can automatically analyze and recommend the correct CPU requests for your pods?
options: Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) in recommendation mode.
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) in optimization mode.
correctAnswers: Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) in recommendation mode.

explanation.general explanation: The Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) can be run in 'Recommendation' mode (or 'Off' mode). It observes the actual CPU and memory usage of pods over time and provides recommendations for what the pod requests and limits should be. This prevents over-provisioning pod manifests.

why other options are wrong.Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) in optim: HPA controls the *number* of pod replicas, not the CPU/Memory sizes inside the pod spec. There is no 'optimization mode'.
NAP creates new node pools based on pod requests, but if the pod requests are artificially inflated (2 vCPU), NAP will just provision unnecessarily large nodes.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine Rightsizing Recommendatio: This applies to raw VMs (GCE instances), not to Kubernetes Pod manifests within a GKE cluster.

questions.questionText: Your company commits to spending at least $50,000 per hour on Compute Engine resources for the next 3 years. However, your engineering teams frequently change from N2 to E2 to C2 machine families depending on project phases. What type of Committed Use Discount (CUD) allows you to secure a discount while retaining the ability to switch machine families globally?

explanation.general explanation: Spend-based (Flexible) CUDs apply a discount to a committed dollar amount of spend per hour. Because it is tied to spend rather than specific hardware (vCPU/RAM), you can freely change machine families (e.g., from N2 to E2) and geographic regions without losing the discount.

why other options are wrong.Resource-based Committed Use Discounts: Resource-based CUDs lock you into specific vCPU and Memory amounts within a specific region and often specific machine families.
why other options are wrong.Sustained Use Discounts (SUDs): SUDs are automatic discounts for running a VM long-term in a month. They do not require a 3-year commitment and offer lower discounts. They also do not apply to newer families like E2.
why other options are wrong.Volume Discounts: While Google offers volume pricing for some services, CUDs are the mechanism for Compute Engine commitments.

questions.questionText: A new project requires deploying a Cloud Storage bucket for temporary application cache data. High availability against a regional failure is strictly NOT required, as the cache can be easily rebuilt. You want to choose the storage location type that minimizes storage and network costs. Which location type should you choose?

explanation.general explanation: A single-region bucket stores data in one specific geographic location. Because the data is not replicated to other regions, it incurs the lowest storage costs. If the workload running in the same region accesses it, there are also zero egress costs.

why other options are wrong.Multi-region: Multi-region provides geographic redundancy across a large area (like 'US' or 'EU') but has higher storage costs.
why other options are wrong.Dual-region: Dual-region pairs two specific regions for high availability, resulting in higher storage costs and replication fees.
why other options are wrong.Edge cache region: This is not a valid Cloud Storage location type; edge caching is handled by Cloud CDN.

questions.questionText: You maintain a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL database used exclusively by QA testers during business hours. To optimize costs over the weekend, you do not want to delete the database, but you want to stop paying for the vCPUs and memory. What action should you take?
options: Change the database tier to shared-core on Friday.
Take a snapshot, delete the instance, and restore it on Monday.
Enable Cloud SQL autoscaling to scale instances to zero.

explanation.general explanation: You can manually or programmatically stop a Cloud SQL instance. When stopped, you are no longer billed for the instance's compute (vCPU and Memory) or pricing. You will only be billed for the persistent storage the data occupies.

why other options are wrong.Change the database tier to shared-core: While this reduces costs, you still pay for a running instance. Stopping it entirely is cheaper.
why other options are wrong.Take a snapshot, delete the instance, an: This involves significant operational overhead, risks data loss if not done perfectly, and changes connection IP strings unnecessarily.
why other options are wrong.Enable Cloud SQL autoscaling to scale in: Cloud SQL does not support scaling to zero instances.

questions.questionText: Over the past year, your developers have spun up and deleted thousands of Compute Engine VMs. You investigate the billing report and notice high ongoing costs for Persistent Disks (PD). What is the most likely cause of this wasted spend?
options: Developers deleted VMs but did not check 'Delete boot disk when instance is deleted', leaving orphaned disks.
Compute Engine automatically upgrades standard PDs to SSDs after 30 days.
Persistent disks charge a higher rate when attached to Spot VMs.
Cloud Storage automatically backs up all deleted PDs, charging archive storage fees.
correctAnswers: Developers deleted VMs but did not check 'Delete boot disk when instance is deleted', leaving orphaned disks.

explanation.general explanation: When a VM is deleted, attached Persistent Disks are only deleted if the 'Delete boot disk' option was selected during creation or explicitly chosen during deletion. Unattached (orphaned) disks continue to incur full storage costs even though no VM is using them.

why other options are wrong.Compute Engine automatically upgrades st: Google Cloud does not automatically change your disk types.
why other options are wrong.Persistent disks charge a higher rate wh: The disk pricing is the same regardless of whether the VM is a standard or Spot VM.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Storage automatically backs up all: There is no automatic feature that backs up deleted PDs to Cloud Storage without explicit configuration (like snapshot schedules).

questions.questionText: You are selecting an App Engine environment for a new Python application. The application will receive highly unpredictable traffic and frequently goes several hours without a single request. You must ensure the environment scales to zero instances to avoid baseline compute costs. Which App Engine environment must you choose?

explanation.general explanation: App Engine Standard scales instances extremely fast (milliseconds) and can scale down to exactly zero instances when there is no incoming traffic. This means you incur zero compute charges during idle hours.

why other options are wrong.App Engine Flexible: App Engine Flexible provisions actual Compute Engine VMs under the hood. It requires at least 1 instance to be running at all times to serve traffic, incurring baseline costs.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine Managed Instance Group: MIGs do not natively 'scale to zero' and hold incoming HTTP traffic gracefully while booting like serverless products do.
why other options are wrong.Google Kubernetes Engine: GKE requires a running cluster and worker nodes; it does not natively scale the entire application footprint to absolute zero cost.

questions.questionText: Your team is building an event-driven architecture using Cloud Functions. You noticed during load testing that a massive burst of events causes Cloud Functions to scale out to thousands of instances simultaneously, depleting backend database connections and causing huge unpredictable bills. How can you limit the cost and concurrent scale of a Cloud Function?
options: Set the `max-instances` flag when deploying the function.
Route all requests through an API Gateway to throttle traffic.
Configure a Cloud Storage lifecycle policy.
Use a Custom Machine Type for the Cloud Function.
correctAnswers: Set the `max-instances` flag when deploying the function.

explanation.general explanation: By setting the `max-instances` limit on a Cloud Function, you cap the number of concurrent instances the service will create. This directly controls your maximum possible cost per minute and protects downstream systems like databases from being overwhelmed.

why other options are wrong.Route all requests through an API Gatewa: While API Gateway can rate limit, setting `max-instances` is the direct, native way to limit the scaling and cost of the Cloud Function itself.
why other options are wrong.Configure a Cloud Storage lifecycle poli: Lifecycle policies deal with object storage retention, not compute scaling.
why other options are wrong.Use a Custom Machine Type for the Cloud: Cloud Functions do not use Custom Machine Types; they use specific memory/CPU allocations (e.g., 256MB, 512MB).

questions.questionText: A university research lab is hosting a 50 TB dataset in Cloud Storage. They want to make this dataset publicly available to other researchers globally. However, the lab has no budget to pay for the massive network egress bandwidth costs that downloading 50 TB repeatedly will incur. What feature should they enable on the bucket?

explanation.general explanation: Enabling 'Requester Pays' on a Cloud Storage bucket shifts the cost of data access and network egress from the bucket owner to the Google Cloud project of the user requesting the data. This allows organizations to share massive datasets without going bankrupt from egress fees.

why other options are wrong.Bucket Lock: Bucket Lock enforces retention policies (WORM compliance) to prevent data deletion; it does not shift billing responsibilities.
why other options are wrong.Object Versioning: Object versioning keeps historical copies of modified files; it actually increases storage costs.
why other options are wrong.Cloud CDN caching: While Cloud CDN reduces egress costs, it still charges the bucket owner for the CDN egress. It does not shift the cost entirely to the downloader.
